newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Little impact seen from Seoul shareholding change.
newsitem.headline: Little impact seen from Seoul shareholding change.

text.p: South Korea on Monday raised the ceiling for foreign share-ownership by three percentage points, but analysts said they saw little short-term impact on the local stock market because of poor fundamentals.
The Finance Ministry said it would raise the aggregate foreign ownership ceiling to 23 percent of a listed company from the current 20 percent, effective from May 1.
Ministry officials said the move, along with other steps to open wider the local capital market, was aimed at attracting foreign funds to put a brake on the local currency's fall.
The announcement was made shortly after the close of trade on Monday, but the share market rallied to end 1.52 percent higher on the belief that an announcement was imminent.
The composite index gained 10.15 points to 677.34.

Analysts welcomed the move, but said immediate beneficiaries would be limited to a handful of blue chips in which foreigners are interested. Most other firms would be ignored unless their economic fundamentals improved, they said.

"I don't think foreigners will turn aggressive (buyers) unless the current account turns around," said Lee Keun-mo, head of research at ING-Baring Securities. "I don't expect much from the announcement."

The ministry said it expected the increased ceiling to bring a further $3 billion into the market, but securities analysts estimated the fresh inflow of funds at between $500 million and $600 million.
Analysts said the country's growing current account deficit and the resulting depreciation of the won are the main factors discouraging foreign investment in local stocks.
The deficit widened to $2.45 billion in February from $1.98 billion a year earlier. Last year, the deficit rose to a record $23.72 billion compared to an $8.95 billion shortfall in 1996.
Namuh Rhee, head of research at Dongbang Peregrine Securities, also played down the likely impact of the expanded ownership ceiling.

"Most of the rebound we saw in the past couple of days reflected the expected increase in the foreign investment limit. Therefore, I think the actual announcement will have a limited impact," Rhee said.
The expansion of the ceiling was in line with South Korea's earlier plan that called for a three-percentage-point increase by the end of this year.

The government had earlier said a further three percentage point rise in the limit would take place in 1998 and 1999, and the ceiling would be removed altogether in 2000. But the Finance Ministry said it was considering further expanding the ceiling within this year.
Analysts said Samsung Electronics Co, SK Telecom Co, Pohang Iron and Steel Co, Kookmin Bank and Shinhan Bank would benefit most from the increased ceiling.
"Foreigners are paying premiums over the counter for these shares," said Rhee.
The aggregate foreign ownership ceiling on "strategically important" Pohang Iron and Korea Electric Power Corp will be raised to 18 percent from the current 15 percent.
At the end of February, foreigners held 989.12 million shares, or 11.43 percent of total listed local shares, according to the Securities Supervisory Board.
